Architecture, as defined by the Webster New International Dictionary (2nd Edition, 1950), encompasses the [a]rt or science of building; A method or style of building; Construction [of a] ... frame or structure; Architectural product. Architecture requires the creation of a product or structure; for the Enterprise Architect, the product is collaboration with the stakeholders.

Stakeholders play a leadership role in driving the business towards its mission. They are involved in all aspects of the business, including defining processes, technology, and the people responsible for executing these processes. The following table identifies key stakeholder groups and their roles within the enterprise architecture practice.

Key Stakeholder Groups in Enterprise Architecture
C-Suite Officers One group of stakeholders is the C-Suite officers. Each department (line, business unit, etc.) has a specific role in the enterprise, and all are dependent on IT in some capacity. The various C-level officers are accountable to the CEO for providing business capabilities (one or more Business Service) which taken together ARE the enterprise. They are entrusted to manage efficiently, ensuring cost-effectiveness and maximum productivity. This group measures success through revenue growth, cost management, competitive positioning, and risk mitigation. The EA practice must translate technical initiatives into these business outcomes.
Business Unit Heads The Business Leaders are another group of stakeholders. They are particularly important stakeholders for the Enterprise Architect. The leaders (and Business Architects if applicable) define the business functions needed to support the business processes. The Enterprise Architecture team works closely with Business Unit Heads to understand their needs and ensure that the business functions align with the overall business strategy. Success for this group is measured through operational efficiency, customer satisfaction, time-to-market, and team productivity. The EA practice must demonstrate how architectural decisions enable these metrics.
Subject Matter Experts This group goes by different names across organziations but the role remains the same: they are the experts on both how the business processes are supported and on the user iterfaces of the application services and structures of the data objects needed to provide the business function. They are invaulable to the architecture practice in understanding what that the Application Service provides, and how the sytesms are used. They are quite knowledgeable about baseline and also aware of user pain points.
Technology Engineers Implement and maintain technology solutions that support business processes and objectives which:
  • Are Secure
  • Are Scalable
  • Are Reliable
  • Are Cost-Effective
Users Utilize the products and services provided by the organization. Provide feedback and requirements to guide business and technology decisions. This group is essential for validating the effectiveness and usability of the enterprise's offerings.

Stakeholder Communication: The Architecture Practice's Critical Skill

While stakeholders have different roles and concerns, successful architecture practices recognize that each stakeholder group requires communication in their own language. Technical architecture diagrams serve IT teams, but C-Suite officers need business cases with ROI projections, business unit heads need process impact assessments, and end users need simple demonstrations of how their work improves. The Enterprise Architect's role is to translate one architectural solution into multiple stakeholder-specific conversations, maintaining consistency while customizing the message to what each group cares about.

AI-Era Stakeholder Considerations

As organizations integrate AI capabilities, stakeholder concerns evolve. C-Suite officers worry about AI risk and competitive positioning. Business leaders question which processes truly benefit from AI. Security teams need assurances about data privacy and model governance. End users fear job displacement. The EA practice must address these AI-specific concerns while maintaining focus on measurable business outcomes.
